sections.value:
**Performance: block** at `253374c27943f039df593a46919ff2ecb2fb1cb1`.

Full PR-owned review against `c3895da518aad2047749b87dc9c6663592e357e2`. No new daemon executable launch site was found, but the held detector can starve its own fleet and busy-turn steering adds recurring work that the per-message/no-new-poll cost claim does not describe.

## Findings

**P152-F001: global LIMIT precedes fleet filtering.** `store/src/held.rs:39-59` orders and limits the global unflagged/old-live delivery union to 50 rows. Only afterward does `pa_watchdog.rs:1052-1073` filter recipients to the PA's fleet. Fifty older foreign holds can occupy every page indefinitely, hiding an eligible local message. They are not marked by that PA, so its next digest sees the same foreign page. This is both a detector failure and repeated global-query work with no useful local result.

Scope both union arms before ordering/limiting. Add a test with at least 50 older foreign holds plus an eligible local hold; the local PA must list/flag its message without touching the foreign ones. The current EXPLAIN test proves partial-index use, not fleet-before-limit semantics or constant query cost.

**P152-F002: terminal polling fans out per steered message.** Each newly consumed message becomes `this.completion` (`store.mjs:1874`), and the next busy claim starts `settleInBackground` for it (`1436-1451,1547-1569`). Earlier completion waits continue until the shared session run ends. Consequently, J unfinished messages create J independent history cursors, wait loops and run-state checks, not one observer per turn.

`waitForObservation` (`1728-1755`) repeatedly reads up to 128 events and backs off from 250 ms to five seconds. Each completion asks `queue.pendingItems` and `metadata.isProcessing` at least every 30 seconds while waiting, and sooner on triggers. Each SDK call also owns a 15-second deadline timer. The one-outstanding-read guard is per completion, not per seat. No hard cap on J is introduced, so repeated steers during a long turn increase idle polling, SDK traffic and retained correlation state. The five-steer canary checks behavior, not this growing RPC/timer budget.

Use one shared terminal/run-state observer per bridge/turn with per-message correlation/reporting metadata. Add a many-steer, still-running-turn test whose read/poll count stays bounded per seat rather than per unfinished message.

**P152-F003: formerly barrier-held busy inboxes activate a 500 ms database poll.** Before this change the receiver waited for its previous message's completion before opening the next inbox claim. With steering on it keeps that claim pending during the busy turn instead. The existing server `claim_inbox_inner` loop reads the recipient and attempts queue ownership, then wakes on an event **or a 500 ms sleep** (`delivery/mod.rs:1629-1661,1893-1904`). Thus an empty inbox in a busy interval that previously had that barrier now adds roughly two timer-driven claim iterations/second per waiting seat, plus event wakes. Idle/user-turn waits that already polled retain their old cost. The timer code is reused, but the newly active portion is not once-per-message work.

Make busy waiting event-driven or obtain an explicit revised AC7/backpressure budget with a validated busy/no-message workload. The 65-second HTTP deadline is an additional existing renewal mechanism, not a bound eliminating the server's half-second polling.

F001/F002 pointers were sent to bobcat. These are source-level findings; no local reproduction was run.

## Other resource shape

| Surface | Cost and limits |
|---|---|
| Claim and switch | One `seat_steering` primary-key read plus schema check per HTTP inbox request, outside the server's internal retry loop. The extension has at most one foreground claim/injection in progress, but F002 adds background observers. Empty/failed long polls can renew, not just messages: client deadline defaults to 65 s and generic delay backs off to five seconds. |
| Turn consumption | One normal message is claimed, injected and acknowledged before the next is consumed. The native host accepts steers on later model rounds; queueing ahead remains. No new OS launch from the JS claim itself, but steering changes current inference work and input content, which a daemon launch counter cannot price. |
| Held digest | One global compound read per generated digest, not every watchdog tick. It walks unflagged-held and live-delivery partial indexes, joins job rows, extracts sender from payload JSON, and orders candidates. LIMIT 50 bounds returned rows, not all global candidate/join/sort work. Post-query fleet matching is up to 50 x fleet-size comparisons. After an admitted digest, shown IDs are upserted in one owned transaction, one statement per shown message. Flagged rows are retained. F001 requires scoping before the page limit. |
| Delivery ack | Every ack adds one primary-key `INSERT ... SELECT` threshold check inside its existing transaction; only a long hold adds a `held_deliveries` row. Existing delivered-ledger insertion/retention remains. Held duration itself uses existing job timestamps, but the flag feature is not zero additional SQL. |
| Limits and replies | Each open, unchecked limited request adds one arrival SELECT with up to three indexed probes; a still-held request adds a registry read. This rides the existing 60-second limit pass. A correlated reply adds a primary-key role-request read and eligible answer update, sharing the existing answered field with output answers. No new limit timer. |
| Receipt note / steer verb | A queued receipt adds a registry lookup, and native busy Copilot may add the steering lookup. Explicit steer on/off reads then upserts even if unchanged; only an actual change emits its audit/FYI. Status reads the explicit-setting inventory and, for a named seat, its setting. These are command-local costs, not background jobs. |

## Canary and proof limits

The documented canary used a real Copilot CLI **1.0.108-1**, native extension, private daemon/store and a deterministic local fixture model. Source was `6108221`; later changes to this final head do not change production files. Five messages reached one running turn, the turn ended, and the seat became idle. Steering off held a later message until turn end.

The displayed timestamps show **claim-to-ack 4, 8, 10, 10, 10 s**, but **queue-to-ack 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 s**: queued steers ahead add rounds. Off-case queue-to-ack was **73 s**. These are fixture observations, not real-provider latency bounds, proof of bounded RPC fanout, or inference-cost measurements. “One round per steer” is consumption pacing, not proof of exactly one additional billable model request.

**CI:** GitHub is CLEAN at this exact head. [CI 42368599513](https://github.com/AI-Substrate/pij-fleet/actions/runs/42368599513) has four successful jobs; latest [delivers 42368921695](https://github.com/AI-Substrate/pij-fleet/actions/runs/42368921695) succeeds. JUnit lists **2,070 executed cases, zero failures/errors**, including held once-only behavior, held/arrival EXPLAIN guards, switch grammar/read/receipt, limit timing, reply answering and all six spawn guards. Five Rust tests were skipped separately. Node 22's native gate passed **326/326**, including both C31 claim/barrier tests. These cases do not cover the three findings above.

## Migration and deployment measurements owed

Current main's schema is 36 and this head compiles schema **38**, so its present ordering is valid. If #153's 0039 lands first, rebase must include that unchanged migration and retain `SCHEMA_VERSION >= 39`. The previously verified SQLx 0.8.6 ledger algorithm applies an absent 0038 even when 0039 already ran, and boot always invokes it before resetting the pragma to the compiled maximum. This unrebased schema-38 binary would refuse a schema-39 store; do not deploy it after 0039 without that integration.

After fixes and authorized deployment, AC1 needs same-cohort queue-to-claim, claim-to-ack and end-to-end distributions, plus pending/failed ages, steering state and busy intervals; do not select only completed successes. AC7 needs matched PID/build launch sites, machine rate, daemon/extension CPU/RSS, busy-empty-inbox claim/SQL rate, SDK read/run-state rate, and observer count versus steers. Use normal authorized work, not a synthetic load storm. The existing BEFORE receipts are historical, not controlled proof that these new CPU/SDK costs are zero.

No local builds, tests, runtime probes, model calls, canary reruns or review-tree edits.
